title: Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services (Dec 2017 TCC) Case
subject: TCC informal-procedure appeal examining contemporaneous records in high-pressure water pipe-liner removal projects.
summary: Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 256, shows Canadian SR&ED claimants that contemporaneous records are decisive. The Tax Court of Canada dismissed the hydrodemolition contractor’s appeal under the Income Tax Act because its vague weekly notes lacked hypotheses and results, and its after-the-fact spreadsheet received no weight under the fifth Northwest Hydraulic test.
metaDescription: Discover the December 2017 Tax Court of Canada ruling for Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services on Canadian SR&ED tax credit claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
1.1 Overview of the Taxpayer’s Claim and Technical Operations

In Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen, 2017 TCC 256 (Docket: 2017-1942(IT)I), handed down in Ottawa on December 22, 2017, Justice David E. Graham of the Tax Court of Canada adjudicated an appeal heard under the Court’s Informal Procedure concerning the eligibility of claimed Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) expenditures and associated Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under the Canadian Income Tax Act (ITA). The appellant, Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. (“Mac & Mac”), operated as a specialized industrial contractor utilizing high-pressure water jetting (hydrodemolition) technologies. The dispute arose after the Minister of National Revenue (the “Minister”), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), reassessed the appellant to deny its claimed SR&ED expenditure deductions and related ITCs in their entirety. As framed by Justice Graham at paragraph [2] of the reasons for judgment, the sole issue before the Court was whether the expenditures incurred by Mac & Mac qualified as SR&ED expenditures within the meaning of the ITA.

The factual matrix of the appeal centred on two sequential industrial engineering projects involving large-diameter metal pipes utilized in the Canadian oil sands sector to transport abrasive bitumen. To protect the structural steel walls of these pipelines from severe erosive and corrosive wear caused by bitumen flow, the interior surfaces of the pipes were lined with a quarter inch of rubber, which was in turn coated by a one-inch polyurethane coating. Specifically, the internal pipe protection system consisted of a dual-layer elastomer configuration comprising a base rubber lining bonded to the interior metal pipe wall, overlaid by an inner polyurethane lining directly exposed to the bitumen stream. Over extended operational cycles, the bitumen travelling through the pipes caused progressive mechanical wear and degradation to the internal lining. As the decision records, this wear to the lining meant that eventually the pipe had to be replaced.

A potential client approached Mac & Mac to see whether the company could develop a method of removing the entire lining from the large metal pipes without damaging the pipe. This commercial inquiry gave rise to two distinct claimed SR&ED projects. The first project sought to develop a method capable of removing the entire lining—encompassing both the one-inch polyurethane coating and the quarter-inch rubber layer—without damaging the pipe. After Mac & Mac eventually succeeded in achieving full lining removal under the first project, the company initiated a second project aimed at a substantially more delicate material-separation objective: developing a method to selectively remove only the polyurethane lining while leaving the rubber lining intact.

During the course of both projects, Mac & Mac tried many different techniques to remove the linings, all of which involved the application of high-pressure water, consistent with its hydrodemolition specialty: hydraulicing, cutting and milling. As detailed in paragraphs [4] through [6] of the decision, the taxpayer began the first project by trying hydraulicing, using two nozzles attached to a device dragged through the pipe, and then varied one parameter at a time, including the angle of spray, the water pressure, the number and size of nozzles, the distance between the nozzles and the linings, the rotation and length of the arms, the spin of the nozzle heads, the speeds of arm rotation and nozzle spin, the speed at which the nozzles moved through the pipe, and the means by which the apparatus was moved through the pipe. Because hydraulicing and cutting would not work for the second project, the appellant had to develop a method of milling, which required a different process from that used in the first project. These trials involved changes such as using two different water pressures at the same time, rotating the pipe itself, altering the number and speed of the passes through the pipe, mounting the apparatus on a long beam instead of wheels, changing the nozzle heads between passes and changing the water pressure between passes, with Mac & Mac again changing only one of these variables at a time.
1.2 The Minister’s Challenge and the Governing Statutory Framework

Under the Canadian federal tax regime, incentives for industrial research and development are administered through a bifurcated statutory mechanism in the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.). First, subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct current expenditures—and, for expenditures incurred before 2014 and again for property acquired after December 15, 2024 under the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3 (assented to March 26, 2026), capital expenditures—incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada, pooling these amounts for immediate deduction or indefinite carry-forward against business income. Second, subsections 127(5) and 127(9) provide for the generation of Investment Tax Credits based on “qualified expenditures” incurred in respect of SR&ED. For a qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC), eligible SR&ED expenditures up to the annual expenditure limit ($3 million for the taxation years at issue, increased to $6 million for tax years beginning after December 15, 2024) earn an enhanced 35% ITC that is 100% refundable for current expenditures, whereas non-qualifying corporations or expenditures exceeding the threshold earn a 15% basic ITC, with 40% refundability available to certain CCPCs on excess current expenditures and a 20-year carry-forward period applying to unused credits.

The foundational gateway to both the section 37 expenditure deduction and the section 127 ITC is the statutory definition of “scientific research and experimental development” codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a “systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis”. The statutory definition enumerates three eligible categories of investigation: basic research (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view), applied research (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view), and experimental development (work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements), alongside eligible support work such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research where such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core research or experimental development. Crucially, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition in subsection 248(1) expressly exclude commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, as well as the commercial use of a new or improved process, routine data collection, quality control, routine testing, market research, and style changes.

Because the statutory language of subsection 248(1) requires judicial interpretation to distinguish genuine experimental development from routine industrial problem-solving, Canadian tax jurisprudence relies on the landmark five-question test articulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), subsequently endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, and embedded in CRA administrative policy. To establish that claimed activities constitute SR&ED, the taxpayer bears the legal burden of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that five cumulative criteria are satisfied. First, the taxpayer must establish that there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the taxpayer must demonstrate that the person claiming to do SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the taxpayer must prove that the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the process must have resulted in a technological advancement, understood as an advancement in the general understanding of scientific or technological relations rather than mere commercial functionality. Fifth, a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and the results obtained, must have been kept as the work progressed.

In auditing and reassessing Mac & Mac, the Minister denied the claimed SR&ED deductions and ITCs for the taxation years ending July 31, 2012 and 2013, placing the eligibility of both pipe-delining projects under subsection 248(1) and the Northwest Hydraulic framework in issue. The reasons for judgment do not record the specific grounds advanced by the CRA at the audit or objection stage; the decision frames the dispute solely as whether the expenditures qualified as SR&ED expenditures, and the Court ultimately resolved that question on the adequacy of the taxpayer’s records of hypotheses, tests and results kept as the work progressed.
1.3 The Court’s Final Holding and Jurisprudential Significance

Justice Graham dismissed Mac & Mac’s appeal in its entirety, upholding the Minister’s denial of the SR&ED deductions and ITCs. Rather than conducting a protracted inquiry into whether the physical delamination of polyurethane and rubber linings from bitumen pipes involved genuine technological uncertainty under the first criterion or sought a valid technological advancement under the fourth criterion, the Court anchored its ratio decidendi squarely on the fifth criterion of the Northwest Hydraulic test. Justice Graham held that the fifth criterion affirmatively required Mac & Mac to have kept a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the experimental results as the work progressed.

Examining the evidentiary record, Justice Graham found that the weekly handwritten notes maintained by Mac & Mac during the project described the tested operational parameters only in vague terms, contained no hypotheses, gave scant details about the changes made and very little information about the results, such that no one, even someone very experienced in the industry, could hope to replicate or confirm Mac & Mac’s results from them. Conversely, while a more detailed spreadsheet was tendered into evidence at trial, it had been prepared after the fact for the purpose of supporting the SR&ED claim rather than contemporaneously as the experiments were conducted, still did not contain the level of detail the Court would have expected, and was given no weight. Relying directly on Justice Bocock’s pronouncement in Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 137 at paragraph 22, Justice Graham concluded that lacking reliable, detailed contemporaneous records of the hypotheses tested and the results obtained as the work progressed, the fifth Northwest Hydraulic test was not met, rendering it impossible for Mac & Mac’s appeal to succeed.

Within Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. represents a pivotal reinforcement of the strict evidentiary gatekeeping trend in the Tax Court of Canada. In the late 1990s—most notably in 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (1998 TCC)—Justice Archambault had observed that because the ITA and its Regulations do not explicitly mandate written technical reports as a statutory condition precedent, a taxpayer could theoretically remedy sparse written documentation through credible, detailed oral testimony at trial. However, the subsequent two decades of TCC decisions—including Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 261, aff’d 2011 FCA 355), Highweb & Page Group Inc. (2015 TCC 137), Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6), and Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. (2017 TCC 256)—have elevated the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion from an administrative guideline to a virtually insurmountable substantive barrier where contemporaneous testing logs are vague or reconstructed ex post facto.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures
2.1 Deficiencies in Contemporaneous Documentation: Vague Weekly Notes Versus Retroactive Spreadsheets

The fatal defect that dismantled Mac & Mac’s appeal lies in the stark dichotomy between the two forms of documentary evidence adduced at trial, analyzed by Justice Graham in paragraphs [8] through [11] of the ruling. Under Canadian tax litigation procedure, ministerial assumptions of fact pleaded in the Reply to the Notice of Appeal are presumed true until demolished by the taxpayer on a balance of probabilities. In SR&ED appeals, demolishing the Minister’s assumption that no systematic investigation occurred requires objective proof of the experimental trajectory.

Mac & Mac tendered two primary documentary artifacts to substantiate its experimental testing on the bitumen pipes. The first artifact consisted of a set of handwritten notes compiled on a weekly basis while the projects were underway. While these notes satisfied the temporal requirement of contemporaneity, they failed the substantive specificity threshold. Justice Graham observed in paragraph [8] that the weekly handwritten notes described the various operational parameters being tested “in only vague terms”. Crucially, the notes contained no hypotheses, so there was no way of telling what Mac & Mac hoped to achieve from the changes; they contained scant details about the changes being made—for example, the notes indicated that different nozzle sizes and angles were tried but did not specify what those sizes or angles were—and they contained very little information about the results of the tests. Consequently, Justice Graham noted that, given the large number of parameters involved, he would have expected the notes to be much more detailed, and that there was simply no way that someone, even someone very experienced in the industry, could hope to replicate or confirm Mac & Mac’s results from those notes.

In addition to the weekly handwritten notes, Mac & Mac also entered a technical spreadsheet into evidence, addressed by the Court in paragraph [9]. Justice Graham acknowledged that this spreadsheet “provided more detail than the notes” regarding the parameters and trials. However, the spreadsheet suffered from the converse defect: it was not prepared contemporaneously as the work progressed, having instead been prepared after the fact for the purpose of supporting the SR&ED claim. Moreover, even this after-the-fact spreadsheet still did not contain the level of detail the Court would have expected, and Justice Graham accordingly gave the spreadsheet no weight at all.

In paragraph [10], Justice Graham anchored his rejection of this evidentiary record in Justice Bocock’s holding in Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 137 at paragraph 22. In the passage quoted from Highweb & Page, the Tax Court emphasized that while evidence of the outcome is important, it is critical to technological advancement that the rigours of adherence to the scientific and experimental method be kept on a detailed and concurrent basis with the conduct of the experiments. Justice Bocock explained that, because a negative answer to the hypothesis is a more frequent outcome and frequently as helpful in advancing technological knowledge, detailed step-by-step logging, analysis and measurement is a mandatory requirement rather than an optional addendum: it is the roadmap which, if one loses the way and failure results, allows one to retrace through accurate records and deduce a different direction, speed or mode. When a taxpayer relies on vague weekly summaries supplemented by a detailed after-the-fact spreadsheet, no such roadmap exists, and the Court is left without any record of what the taxpayer hoped to achieve from changes such as new nozzle heads or water pressures between passes, or of what results those changes produced.
2.2 Failure to Substantiate a Systematic Investigation Versus Routine Trial-and-Error

A deeper structural analysis of Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. reveals that failing the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion is rarely an isolated clerical oversight; instead, it is often the evidentiary symptom of a failure to conduct a genuinely “systematic investigation or search… by means of experiment or analysis” under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, although in Mac & Mac itself the Court expressly found it unnecessary to consider whether the other Northwest Hydraulic tests were met. In industrial and mechanical engineering environments, the boundary between eligible experimental development and ineligible “trial and error” or routine engineering optimization is policed strictly through the discipline of the scientific method under the second and third criteria of Northwest Hydraulic.

In paragraphs [4] through [6], Justice Graham recounted that Mac & Mac “tried many different techniques to remove the linings,” all of which involved the application of high-pressure water—hydraulicing, cutting and milling—starting the first project with hydraulicing and, for the second project, developing a milling method whose variations included “changing nozzle heads between passes, and changing the water pressure between passes”. Importantly, the Court also recorded that in both projects Mac & Mac changed only one of these variables at a time. In Canadian SR&ED law, “trying many different techniques” does not by itself establish a systematic investigation; what the Court faulted in Mac & Mac was not the sequencing of the trials but the absence of any recorded hypotheses, specific parameter values and results. To constitute a systematic investigation adhering to the scientific method, each experimental iteration must begin with a formal, falsifiable hypothesis—defined by the Tax Court in the contemporaneous decision Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, as “a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial” that predicts a specific causal relationship between controlled independent variables and dependent physical outcomes.

The parallel between Mac & Mac (decided December 2017) and Joel Theatrical Rigging (decided January 2017) illuminates the Tax Court’s analytical posture toward mechanical contractors. In Joel Theatrical Rigging, the taxpayer sought to develop a system for controlling the rate of descent of a theatre fire curtain and conducted physical trials, but failed to measure the exact weight of the curtain, the precise duration of the experiment, or the quantitative rate of the curtain’s descent, and lacked professional engineers or degreed researchers on the research team. The Court held that if the scientific method had been employed—requiring systematic observation, precise measurement, and controlled experimentation—those physical metrics would have been measured and recorded at the time of each trial so that subsequent design modifications could be analytically derived from prior test data. Proper record-keeping is the most reliable means of distinguishing a systematic scientific process from random “trial and error” by clearly outlining hypotheses and potential designs, results from testing and experiments, and modifications to original designs.

Similarly, in Mac & Mac, the Court’s concern was that the notes did not specify what the nozzle sizes and angles tested actually were, contained no hypotheses explaining what Mac & Mac hoped to achieve from each change, and said very little about the results, so that no one could replicate or confirm the results from the records. Although the Court accepted that Mac & Mac changed only one variable at a time, a sequence of single-variable changes whose settings, purposes and outcomes are summarized only in vague weekly handwritten notes cannot be reconstructed or verified after the fact. Even if the operator eventually strips the polyurethane lining while leaving the rubber lining intact, achieving a successful technical or commercial outcome does not, without the detailed records of hypotheses, tests and results required by the fifth Northwest Hydraulic test, permit the claim to succeed.

Furthermore, as demonstrated in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261 (per Justice D’Arcy), aff’d 2011 FCA 355, even where a taxpayer provides sufficient documentation showing that it undertook a systematic investigation, the claim will still fail if the work merely applies existing engineering knowledge and standard equipment adjustments rather than proving technological risk or achieving a technological advancement. In Mac & Mac, because the contemporaneous notes described the tested parameters only in vague terms and contained no hypotheses, the fifth test was not met, and the Court expressly found it unnecessary to consider whether the remaining Northwest Hydraulic tests—including those concerning technological uncertainty and advancement—were satisfied.
2.3 Technological Uncertainty and Advancement in Multi-Layer Material Delamination

From a technical tax advisory standpoint, the central irony of Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. is that the underlying engineering challenge—particularly in the second project—possessed the technical hallmarks of genuine technological uncertainty under the first Northwest Hydraulic criterion, had it been properly framed, investigated, and documented.

In the first project, the objective was to remove the entire lining (both the one-inch polyurethane coating and the quarter-inch rubber layer) from the interior of large metal bitumen pipes without damaging the pipe. Mac & Mac began with hydraulicing—using a water jet to pierce through the material so that large pieces are removed when the water rebounds from the hard surface behind it—and varied the spray angles, water pressures, nozzle number and size, standoff distance, arm and nozzle rotation, and traverse speed one variable at a time until it succeeded in this goal. Because steel possesses a vastly higher yield strength and erosion resistance than elastomers, full removal down to bare metal primarily involved overcoming energy-absorption damping within the combined elastomer layers.

The second project, however, introduced a classic system-level technological uncertainty: selectively ablating and delaminating the inner polyurethane wear layer while leaving the underlying rubber lining completely intact and structurally sound. In polymer physics and fluid dynamics, polyurethane and vulcanized rubber exhibit closely overlapping viscoelastic properties, acoustic impedances, and tensile or tear moduli compared to a polymer-steel interface. When an ultra-high-pressure water jet impinges upon a polyurethane layer bonded to a rubber substrate, the kinetic energy required to fracture and shear the cross-linked polyurethane matrix (σ ≈ 40 MPa) readily propagates across the interfacial bond boundary, causing cavitation micro-pitting, cohesive tearing, or thermal degradation within the underlying rubber layer (σ ≈ 20 MPa). Moreover, operating inside a long, enclosed bitumen pipe meant that standoff distance, jet impingement angle, nozzle rotation harmonics, and multi-pass hydraulic backwash interacted non-linearly with variations in bitumen-worn polyurethane thickness.

To articulate this as a valid technological uncertainty under Northwest Hydraulic, Mac & Mac needed to establish its baseline industry knowledge base, demonstrating why standard hydrodemolition pressure tables, off-the-shelf rotary nozzle specifications, and routine operator adjustments could not predict or control selective interfacial delamination between two bonded elastomers. However, because Mac & Mac’s contemporaneous notes did not specify the parameters tested, contained no hypotheses and recorded very little about the results, the technical narrative available to the Court was limited to the general list of variations recounted in paragraphs [4] through [6], from hydraulicing with two nozzles to milling with changes in pipe rotation, pass count and speed, beam mounting, nozzle heads and water pressure. Because the fifth Northwest Hydraulic test was not met, the Court did not reach the question of whether a technological advancement under the fourth criterion—defined as the generation of new scientific or technological knowledge that advances the existing baseline of technology—had been achieved, and nothing in the decision should be read as a finding either way on that point.
2.4 Commercial and Contractual Considerations: Client-Initiated R&D and Shop-Floor Cost Segregation

Beyond the scientific eligibility criteria of Northwest Hydraulic, the factual background of Mac & Mac highlights critical commercial, contractual, and financial accounting pitfalls that routinely trigger CRA audit disallowances under subsections 248(1), 37(1), and 127(9) of the ITA. Justice Graham specifically noted that Mac & Mac “was approached by a potential client to see if Mac & Mac” could develop a method of removing the entire lining from its bitumen transport pipes without damaging the pipe. When industrial R&D is initiated in response to a specific client inquiry and executed on physical assets such as worn bitumen pipes (the decision does not record whether the pipes used in Mac & Mac’s trials were supplied by the client), two acute legal risks arise under the Canadian SR&ED regime, although the Court in Mac & Mac made no finding on either point because the appeal was resolved on the fifth Northwest Hydraulic test alone.

First, under paragraph (i) of the SR&ED definition in subsection 248(1), work performed in the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process, is statutorily excluded from eligibility. Where a contractor cleans or delines a client’s pipes on the shop floor, the CRA routinely takes the position that once a viable parameter set is identified—or if the contractor is simultaneously cleaning multiple pipes for commercial delivery—the activity constitutes commercial pipe-cleaning services or commercial production rather than experimental development. Second, under the definitions of “qualified expenditure” and “contract payment” in subsection 127(9) and the expenditure reduction rules in subsection 37(1) of the ITA, if a taxpayer is paid or entitled to be paid by a taxable Canadian supplier or client to perform SR&ED on its behalf, or if the client pays for the delining service under a commercial service contract that effectively funds the underlying development work, the amount of the contract payment or non-government assistance must be deducted from the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool, eliminating the claimant’s entitlement to ITCs on those funded costs.

Furthermore, as highlighted in the CRA’s standard audit objections cited in the scholarship reviewing Mac & Mac, a claimant’s failure to maintain detailed daily records renders “the nature and extent of the work conducted in the tax period… not clear”. In Highweb & Page Group Inc. and related jurisprudence such as Danat and Zeuter Development, the Tax Court has underscored that inadequate contemporaneous documentation not only destroys scientific eligibility under the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion, but also prevents the Court from verifying the quantum of salary and material expenditures directly attributable to SR&ED versus commercial shop operations. Although the Court in Mac & Mac made no finding on quantum, weekly handwritten notes that vaguely mention parameter testing are unlikely to substantiate the exact hours spent by operators on experimental passes versus routine equipment setup, maintenance, or commercial pipe refurbishment.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each governing statutory and jurisprudential requirement under Canadian SR&ED law against the specific evidentiary or technical failures identified in Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 256) and the corresponding standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof

cells: Overarching Statutory Definition of SR&ED
Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 248(1) (“systematic investigation or search… by means of experiment or analysis”).

The taxpayer tried many different techniques (hydraulicing, cutting and milling, all using high-pressure water) on bitumen pipe linings, changing one variable at a time, but its records contained no hypotheses, scant details of the changes made and very little information about results, so the systematic structure of the work could not be verified from the records.
The taxpayer must establish on a balance of probabilities that the work transcended empirical “trial and error” and followed a planned, structured sequence of experimentation or engineering analysis.
Criterion 1: Technological Risk or Uncertainty
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC); Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6.

Not adjudicated: the Court found it unnecessary to consider whether the technological uncertainty test was met for full lining removal (Project 1) or selective polyurethane-over-rubber removal (Project 2), because it was clear that the fifth test was not met.
Must prove the existence of a system-level or fundamental technical capability gap that cannot be resolved by routine engineering, standard procedures, or publicly available industrial knowledge.
Criterion 2: Formulation of Specific Hypotheses
Northwest Hydraulic, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC); Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6; Jentel Manufacturing, 2011 TCC 261.

The weekly notes contained no hypotheses, leaving no way of telling what Mac & Mac hoped to achieve from changes such as different nozzle sizes and angles; the Court did not separately rule on this criterion.
Requires explicit, falsifiable technical statements formulated prior to each test run, defining the postulated causal relationship between independent variables and target physical phenomena.
Criterion 3: Total Discipline of the Scientific Method
Northwest Hydraulic, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC); Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6.

Although the Court accepted that Mac & Mac changed only one variable at a time in its iterative adjustments (“changing nozzle heads between passes, and changing the water pressure between passes”), the notes did not specify the values tested (such as nozzle sizes and angles) or the results obtained, so adherence to the scientific method could not be verified from the records; the Court did not separately rule on this criterion.

Testing protocols must isolate variables, systematically measure exact input parameters and output metrics during each trial, and analytically modify subsequent hypotheses based on quantified test results.
Criterion 4: Technological Advancement
Northwest Hydraulic, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC); Jentel Manufacturing, 2011 TCC 261.
Not adjudicated: Mac & Mac succeeded in the practical goal of removing the lining, but the Court expressly declined to consider the technological advancement test once the fifth test had failed.

Must prove that the investigation yielded new scientific or technological knowledge that advances the technological baseline, distinguishing a technological advance from a merely commercial or functional success.
Criterion 5: Detailed Contemporaneous Record-Keeping (Dispositive Issue)
Northwest Hydraulic, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC); Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 137 at para. 22; Mac & Mac, 2017 TCC 256 at paras. 8–11.

Weekly handwritten notes described tested parameters “in only vague terms”, contained no hypotheses and gave very little information about test results. A more detailed spreadsheet entered into evidence was given no weight because it was prepared after the fact for the purpose of supporting the SR&ED claim and still lacked the level of detail the Court expected.

Mandatory retention of detailed, intelligible, contemporaneous records generated as the work progresses, capturing the scientific thought process, exact parameters tested, and quantitative results; ex post facto reconstructions carry negligible weight.
Nature, Extent & Quantum of Eligible Work in the Tax Period
Income Tax Act, ss. 37(1), 127(5), 127(9), 248(1)(e)–(k); Highweb & Page, 2015 TCC 137.

Not addressed by the Court: the decision makes no finding on the segregation of experimental passes from routine commercial hydrodemolition operations or client-funded pipe refurbishment, nor on the quantum of expenditures, as the appeal was dismissed on the record-keeping test alone.

Contemporaneous time-tracking and project cost accounting must clearly demarcate when experimental development begins and ends, excluding commercial production, routine testing, and contract-funded services.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian industrial taxpayers and their tax advisors can proactively inoculate R&D projects against the exact legal and evidentiary disqualifications established in Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 256), the following two applied case studies model realistic industrial scenarios in heavy engineering and surface processing. Each case study exhibits the precise vulnerabilities that defeated Mac & Mac—vague weekly shop notes, retroactive spreadsheet compilation, and unrecorded multi-pass parameter adjustments—together with the client-initiated commercial overlap that the facts of the decision raise but on which the Court did not need to rule, and details a comprehensive, four-pillar remediation architecture compliant with the Income Tax Act and Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence.
4.1 Case Study 1: Selective Cryogenic-Hydrojet Delamination of Fluoropolymer-Lined Sour Gas Autoclave Vessels (Industrial Remediation & Mechanical Engineering)
Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

PetroClean Industrial Dynamics Ltd. (“PetroClean”), a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) based in Edmonton, Alberta, specializes in high-pressure industrial vessel remediation. A major oil sands upgrader approaches PetroClean to determine whether it can refurbish worn, large-diameter carbon-steel transfer conduits and autoclave headers used in high-temperature sour bitumen desulfurization. The interior of these conduits features a dual-layer barrier consisting of a 6 mm (0.24 in) bromobutyl rubber corrosion membrane vulcanized to the steel wall, overlaid by a 3 mm sintered polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) inner wear liner. Sour bitumen slurry erodes and blisters the inner PTFE liner within 36 months, while the underlying bromobutyl rubber layer remains chemically intact. Complete mechanical stripping destroys both layers, costing the client $450,000 per conduit section in full relining.

PetroClean initiates an internal project to selectively strip the degraded PTFE inner liner while leaving the 6 mm bromobutyl rubber substrate intact and free of micro-fissures. Initially, PetroClean’s shop crew tries standard warm-water hydrodemolition and mechanical rotary scraping, which either fails to shear the sintered PTFE or rips straight through the bromobutyl rubber. The crew then begins experimenting with liquid-nitrogen pre-chilling followed by multi-pass ultra-high-pressure (UHP) water jetting, swapping out fan and rotary nozzle heads between passes and adjusting pump pressures between passes. The shop foreman writes weekly Friday summary notes in a coil notebook stating that the crew tried cryogenic chilling with a third rotary head and raised water pressure on passes two and three, achieving better stripping but encountering some rubber pitting. Eight months later, when PetroClean’s external SR&ED consultant prepares the Form T661 claim, the lead engineer reconstructs a detailed 45-row Excel spreadsheet from memory and pump manuals. Under Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. (2017 TCC 256), this claim faces certain disallowance under the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion.
Step 1: Project Governance & Scientific Discipline Restructuring

To transform ad hoc shop-floor adjustments into a statutorily compliant “systematic investigation or search” under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, PetroClean must establish a formal SR&ED Governance Charter prior to commencing physical trials on the conduit sections. First, taking a lesson from Joel Theatrical Rigging (2017 TCC 6), where the Tax Court scrutinized the absence of professional engineers or degreed researchers directing the experimental methodology, PetroClean must appoint a Professional Engineer (P.Eng.) or senior polymer specialist as Principal Investigator to oversee the shop technicians.

Second, the Principal Investigator must formally document the Technological Baseline and Literature Search before the first experimental pass is executed. This baseline report must document standard OEM hydrodemolition pressure curves alongside published tensile and shear moduli of PTFE versus bromobutyl rubber at ambient and cryogenic temperatures, explaining why routine engineering cannot resolve the interfacial delamination problem. Specifically, the governance charter defines the Technological Uncertainty in system-level physical terms: because the adhesive bond strength at the PTFE-bromobutyl interface (≈ 8 MPa) exceeds the cohesive tear threshold of bromobutyl rubber at ambient temperatures (≈ 6 MPa), standard hydrodynamic shear jets inevitably propagate fracture planes into the rubber substrate. The charter establishes that inducing a differential ductile-to-brittle glass transition gradient across the 3 mm PTFE layer via transient cryogenic quenching without embrittling the underlying bromobutyl rubber (which exhibits a glass transition temperature Tg ≈ −65 °C) involves coupled thermodynamic and hydrodynamic variables that cannot be predicted by standard engineering formulas.
Step 2: Technical Documentation & Contemporaneous Data Architecture

To directly overcome Justice Graham’s holdings in paragraphs [8] through [10] of Mac & Mac and Justice Bocock’s strictures in Highweb & Page Group Inc. (2015 TCC 137 at para. 22), PetroClean must abolish weekly retrospective handwritten notes and prohibit post-hoc spreadsheet reconstruction. In their place, PetroClean must deploy a Contemporaneous Pass-by-Pass Digital Experimental Log integrated directly into its shop-floor Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) and Quality Management System (QMS), where every entry is automatically date-and-time-stamped and locked with an immutable cryptographic hash and supervisor digital signature at the conclusion of each pass.

Crucially, the data architecture must compel the operator and Principal Investigator to complete three sequential data blocks in real time for every single experimental pass. First, a Pre-Pass Hypothesis Block must be locked before the high-pressure pump is engaged, stating the exact mathematical and physical hypothesis being tested and identifying which single independent variable is being modified from the immediately preceding pass. Second, an Automated Parameter Capture Block must record exact quantitative test parameters, replacing vague notes about changing water pressures and nozzle heads with exact measurements such as water pressure 120 MPa, nozzle model Rotopulse-4Orifice-0.6mm, impingement angle 45°, traverse velocity 6 mm/s, cryogenic quench duration 1.5 s, and surface temperature −150 °C. Third, a Post-Pass Quantitative Result and Analytical Conclusion Block must be recorded immediately upon pass completion using calibrated ultrasonic thickness gauges to measure remaining PTFE thickness and rubber substrate loss in micrometres alongside Shore A durometer readings, followed by an explicit analytical note explaining whether the hypothesis was falsified or corroborated and how that finding dictates parameter selection for the next pass.
Step 3: Contractual Structuring & Intellectual Property / Risk Allocation under the ITA

Because PetroClean was approached by an oil sands client with worn conduits, PetroClean must insulate its SR&ED claim from commercial service disallowances under paragraph (i) of the SR&ED definition in subsection 248(1) and contract payment reductions under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Rather than accepting a standard commercial Purchase Order to clean and strip four autoclave conduits, PetroClean’s legal counsel must execute a bespoke Experimental Test Piece Bailment and R&D Risk-Allocation Agreement prior to receiving the scrap conduit sections.

Under this contractual structure, the client provides decommissioned, scrap lined conduit sections solely as zero-value bailment test articles for destructive and non-destructive testing, and PetroClean charges zero dollars to the client during the experimental phase, ensuring that no “contract payment” or commercial service revenue is received or receivable under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Furthermore, any commercial service engagement in a future phase is made strictly contingent upon PetroClean first proving technical feasibility and achieving a strict quantitative specification (≥ 98% PTFE removal with less than 50 µm bromobutyl abrasion across 1 m² of continuous surface area). If the experimental trials damage the rubber lining, PetroClean bears 100% of its labour, overhead, and consumable costs with zero reimbursement right. Finally, the contract stipulates that all intellectual property, patent rights, proprietary process parameter envelopes, and custom nozzle designs generated during the investigation vest exclusively in PetroClean, confirming that the SR&ED is undertaken on PetroClean’s own account rather than as a fee-for-service contractor.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking, Hypothesis Formulation, and Financial Cost Segregation

To satisfy CRA financial auditors and prevent the disallowance of labour and material claims due to an unclear “nature and extent of the work conducted in the tax period”, PetroClean must implement a strict Activity-Based SR&ED Cost Segregation Protocol under section 37 of the ITA. Physical testing is restricted to dedicated 300 mm ring coupons cut from a sacrificial conduit rather than full commercial pipeline strings, preventing the CRA from characterizing the passes as commercial production runs under paragraph (i) of the SR&ED definition in subsection 248(1). Shop technicians log their hours using biometric badge-ins tied directly to specific Experimental Trial IDs (EXP-01-P1 through EXP-01-P18), segregating eligible experimental setup, testing, and ultrasonic measurement hours from routine shop maintenance or commercial hydrodemolition jobs. Once the optimal parameter envelope is validated at the conclusion of the experimental series, the Principal Investigator signs a formal Protocol Freeze and Commercial Handover Certificate, terminating SR&ED time-charging immediately before any commercial client conduits are processed.

The table below illustrates the exact structure of PetroClean’s Contemporaneous Digital Experimental Log, demonstrating how each field remedies the fatal evidentiary defects identified in paragraphs [8] and [9] of Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc..

cells: EXP-01-P1 (2026-03-10 09:14:22 MST; Signed: J. Doe, P.Eng.)

H1: Ambient UHP water jetting at 250 MPa with a 15° rotating nozzle will shear the 3 mm PTFE layer via radial hydro-wedging without exceeding the 6 MPa tear modulus of the underlying 6 mm bromobutyl rubber.
Nozzle: Rotopulse-2Orifice-0.8mm; Impingement Angle: 15°; Water Pressure: 250 MPa; Traverse Rate: 10 mm/s; Pre-Chill: None (surface 22 °C).

PTFE Removed: 64% (1.1 mm residual); Rubber Substrate Damage: Severe localized gouging up to 2.4 mm depth where jet penetrated PTFE blisters; Ultrasonic Bond Check: 18% interfacial debonding of rubber from steel.

H1 Falsified: At ambient temperature, PTFE plastic deformation absorbs jet energy until localized breakthrough occurs, at which point 250 MPa stagnation pressure instantly ruptures the viscoelastic rubber substrate. Must induce brittle fracture in PTFE at lower water pressure.
EXP-01-P2 (2026-03-10 13:42:09 MST; Signed: J. Doe, P.Eng.)

H2: Pre-quenching the inner PTFE surface with liquid nitrogen (LN₂) for 8 s to reach −150 °C will depress PTFE fracture toughness by ≈ 60%, allowing clean brittle spallation at a reduced water pressure of 140 MPa while thermal resistance of PTFE keeps the rubber interface above −40 °C.
Nozzle: FanJet-4Orifice-0.5mm; Impingement Angle: 0°; Water Pressure: 140 MPa; Traverse Rate: 8 mm/s; Pre-Chill: LN₂ spray 8 s (surface −150 °C; Interface −58 °C).
PTFE Removed: 92% (0.24 mm residual); Rubber Substrate Damage: Brittle micro-cracking across 35% of rubber surface (up to 0.3 mm depth); Shore A hardness spiked from 65 to 82 during pass.

H2 Partially Falsified: Cryo-quenching enabled low-pressure (140 MPa) PTFE fracture, but 8 s quench conducted excessive thermal flux into the bromobutyl boundary (−58 °C, approaching Tg ≈ −65 °C), causing brittle rubber micro-cracking under jet impact.
EXP-01-P3 (2026-03-11 10:05:47 MST; Signed: J. Doe, P.Eng.)

H3: Limiting pulsed LN₂ quench to 2 × 1.5 s (establishing a steep thermal Biot gradient where PTFE surface reaches −150 °C while rubber interface remains above −25 °C) combined with a 45° high-shear acoustic nozzle at 120 MPa will cleave PTFE along the bond line while rubber retains elastic damping.
Nozzle: AcousticShear-6Orifice-0.4mm; Impingement Angle: 45°; Water Pressure: 120 MPa; Traverse Rate: 6 mm/s; Pre-Chill: Pulsed LN₂ 2 × 1.5 s (surface −150 °C; Interface −22 °C).
PTFE Removed: 99.2% (24 µm residual); Rubber Substrate Damage: Zero micro-cracking; surface profile roughness Ra ≈ 12 µm (ideal for recoating); 0% rubber-to-steel debonding.

H3 Corroborated / Technological Advancement Achieved: Established non-linear coupled thermo-hydrodynamic relationship governing selective fluoropolymer-elastomer delamination via transient thermal gradient isolation (ΔT ≈ 128 °C across the 3 mm PTFE layer) and high-angle shear jetting.

body.text: 4.2 Case Study 2: Multi-Pass Laser-Acoustic Cladding and Slag Ablation for Bitumen Slurry Hydrotransport Impellers (Advanced Metallurgy & Process Automation)
Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

Northern Wearplate & Hydro-Metallurgy Inc. (“Northern Wearplate”), a medium-sized industrial remanufacturer operating in Fort McMurray, Alberta and Mississauga, Ontario, refurbishes heavy-duty centrifugal slurry pump impellers used in oil sands hydrotransport pipelines. These high-chromium white-iron impellers are coated with an ultra-hard 0.5 mm tungsten-carbide cobalt-chromium (WC-10Co-4Cr) cermet layer over a ductile nickel-alloy buffer layer (1.2 mm). During bitumen hydrotransport, silica sand and bitumen erode the WC-10Co-4Cr coating unevenly. To remanufacture the impellers without melting or thermally cracking the underlying nickel-alloy buffer layer and high-chromium base casting, Northern Wearplate attempts to develop a hybrid pulsed-fiber-laser and ultra-high-pressure waterjet stripping head under an internal initiative designated as Project Dual-Ablate.

During shop trials, operators run multiple stripping passes across worn impeller vanes, manually tweaking laser pulse frequencies, waterjet pressures, and nozzle standoff distances between passes. Because the trials occur on the active remanufacturing floor using client-owned impellers sent in for commercial overhaul, operators simply jot down brief weekly remarks on shop travelers noting that during Week 14 they tried three passes on Impeller 402, changed the laser frequency and water nozzle, and were still cracking the nickel layer. At year-end, the plant manager exports commercial ERP job-costing sheets and adds estimated parameter columns to create an SR&ED summary table. Under Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. (2017 TCC 256) and Highweb & Page Group Inc. (2015 TCC 137), this project is fatally exposed to complete denial for lacking contemporaneous experimental records, failing to demonstrate the scientific method, and commingling SR&ED with commercial repair work.
Step 1: Project Governance & Scientific Discipline Restructuring

Northern Wearplate must immediately restructure its project governance to separate scientific experimentation from shop-floor production troubleshooting. The company must constitute an SR&ED Technical Steering Committee led by its Chief Metallurgical Engineer, establishing a formal Design of Experiments (DoE) Protocol prior to any machine trials.

Rather than permitting operators to adjust multiple machine settings simultaneously between passes—which violates the scientific method by confounding independent variables, a defect that the Court in Mac & Mac notably did not find, having accepted that Mac & Mac changed only one variable at a time—the DoE Protocol enforces strict variable isolation across structured experimental phases. First, the Steering Committee formally documents the Technological Uncertainty, explaining why standard laser ablation and abrasive waterjet milling cannot selectively remove WC-10Co-4Cr cermet (Vickers hardness ≈ 1,200 HV) from a 1.2 mm Inconel-625 buffer layer (≈ 250 HV) on complex three-dimensional involute impeller geometries. Specifically, high-fluence laser pulses sufficient to vaporize the cobalt-chromium binder induce tensile thermal shock cracks in the high-chromium cast iron substrate, whereas abrasive garnet waterjets experience severe kerf deflection when transitioning from hard WC carbides to ductile nickel, gouging the buffer layer within milliseconds. Second, the DoE Protocol mandates a Hypothesis-Driven Fractional Factorial Matrix in which every experimental trial series tests a specific mathematical hypothesis coupling laser thermal softening depth (δ ≈ 20–80 µm) with pure non-abrasive waterjet droplet impact pressure, ensuring that nozzle standoff, traverse rate, and laser pulse duration are modified systematically according to a pre-defined factorial matrix rather than operator intuition.
Step 2: Technical Documentation & Contemporaneous Data Architecture

To eliminate the evidentiary vulnerabilities identified by Justice Graham in paragraphs [8] through [11] of Mac & Mac, Northern Wearplate must replace weekly handwritten shop-traveler notes and year-end ERP spreadsheets with an automated Real-Time Telemetry and Metallographic Audit Trail. The hybrid laser-waterjet cell’s Data Acquisition (DAQ) system is configured to export a time-stamped telemetry log at 1 kHz for every experimental pass, recording actual pump pressure, nozzle orifice identification, standoff distance, laser peak power, pulse repetition rate, and traverse velocity.

Before the CNC cycle starts, the metallurgical engineer must enter the specific Pre-Trial Hypothesis into a cloud-based Electronic Lab Notebook (ELN) that applies an immutable trusted timestamp. Immediately after the pass concludes, the telemetry file is linked to the ELN entry alongside quantitative metallographic results, including eddy-current coating thickness scans, dye-penetrant crack counts per square centimetre, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) cross-sectional micrographs of the WC-10Co-4Cr and Inconel interface. When the CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) conducts the technical review, Northern Wearplate submits the raw, unedited ELN logs and DAQ telemetry files generated during the taxation year, completely bypassing the Mac & Mac paragraph [9] retroactive spreadsheet trap.
Step 3: Contractual Structuring & Intellectual Property / Risk Allocation under the ITA

To prevent the CRA from disqualifying the impeller trials as commercial refurbishment services under paragraph (i) of the SR&ED definition in subsection 248(1) or reducing qualified expenditures by commercial overhaul fees under subsection 127(9), Northern Wearplate must sever its experimental development from its commercial customer contracts. Northern Wearplate must never conduct experimental parameter passes on an impeller currently subject to a commercial customer repair work order. Instead, Northern Wearplate purchases and acquires unencumbered legal title to scrapped, unserviceable impellers from oil sands operators under a Scrap Asset Bill of Sale for nominal scrap metal value ($250 per unit), transferring full ownership and risk of loss to Northern Wearplate before any experimental work commences. Furthermore, if an oil sands client wishes to pilot the new laser-waterjet stripping process, the contract is structured as a conditional Future Commercial Supply Agreement where the client pays strictly for finished, specification-compliant refurbished impellers after the R&D project concludes and commercial production begins, with zero non-refundable upfront engineering fees or milestone reimbursements that could be construed as government or non-government assistance or contract payments under subsections 127(9) and 37(1) of the ITA.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking, Hypothesis Formulation, and Financial Cost Segregation

Finally, to satisfy the Tax Court’s strict expenditure substantiation standards articulated in Highweb & Page Group Inc. (2015 TCC 137) and Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. (2017 TCC 256), Northern Wearplate implements a two-tier financial tracking protocol. Every hour claimed under subsection 37(1) for engineers and CNC technicians must reference a specific ELN Hypothesis and Trial ID (ELN-2026-DA-001 through ELN-2026-DA-042) logged on the exact day the work occurred. Any shop time spent on standard impeller sandblasting, commercial re-cladding, or routine machine maintenance is booked to non-SR&ED cost centres. Simultaneously, all sacrificial impeller vanes, custom-machined sapphire waterjet orifices, and metallographic sectioning consumables are requisitioned exclusively under the internal R&D project code and physically retained in an R&D quarantine locker as physical audit exhibits for the CRA RTA.

The following comparative governance table summarizes how Northern Wearplate’s remediated architecture systematically resolves every deficiency that led to the dismissal of the taxpayer’s appeal in Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. v. The Queen.

headers: Deficient Practice in Mac & Mac (2017 TCC 256)
Remediated TCC-Compliant Protocol Implemented by Taxpayer

cells: Frequency & Timing of Technical Records
Compiled handwritten notes only on a weekly summary basis; prepared a more detailed spreadsheet after the fact for the purpose of supporting the SR&ED claim, which the Court gave no weight.
Pass-by-pass real-time ELN entries paired with automated 1 kHz machine DAQ telemetry logs, cryptographically timestamped immediately upon pass completion.
Satisfies the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion and Highweb & Page Group Inc. (2015 TCC 137 at para. 22) requiring contemporaneous records kept as work progresses.
Granularity of Parameter & Result Recording

Described tested parameters “in only vague terms” (for example, indicating that different nozzle sizes and angles were tried without specifying what those sizes or angles were), contained no hypotheses, and gave very little information about the results of the tests.

Records exact independent variables (pressure in MPa, orifice geometry, impingement angle in degrees, traverse rate in mm/s, laser fluence) and quantitative dependent metrics (ultrasonic thickness in µm, crack density, bond shear in MPa).
Satisfies Criteria 3 and 5 of Northwest Hydraulic and Joel Theatrical Rigging (2017 TCC 6) by proving systematic measurement rather than unmeasured trial and error.
Experimental Methodology & Variable Control

Tried multiple techniques (hydraulicing, cutting, milling, nozzle changes, pressure changes), changing only one variable at a time, but without any documented hypotheses stating what each change was expected to achieve.
Enforces a formal Design of Experiments (DoE) protocol where each pass tests an explicit, falsifiable pre-pass hypothesis isolating coupled thermo-mechanical variables.
Satisfies subsection 248(1) (“systematic investigation or search… by means of experiment or analysis”) and Criteria 1, 2, and 3 of Northwest Hydraulic.
Commercial vs. Experimental Demarcation

Initiated work upon a potential client’s inquiry to develop a method of removing the lining from bitumen transport pipes; the decision records no documentary demarcation between experimental trials and commercial service delivery, although the Court made no finding on this point.

Executes a zero-consideration Bailment Agreement or Scrap Asset Bill of Sale on sacrificial coupons, ring-fencing R&D trials from commercial contracts and halting claims via a Protocol Freeze Certificate.

Prevents exclusion under paragraph (i) of the SR&ED definition in subsection 248(1) (commercial production) and preserves full qualified expenditures and ITCs under subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the ITA.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; weekly notes lacked hypotheses, tested parameters, and results, failing the fifth Northwest Hydraulic test.
